chunks.title: Lens anatomy, accommodation & presbyopia
chunks.tldr: Capsule = basement membrane; equatorial epithelium divides for life → new fibres pile outside, old fibres compressed into the nucleus; younger fibres = cortex. Avascular, no nerves, fed by aqueous, anaerobic metabolism. Accommodation: ciliary muscle contracts → zonules relax → lens rounds up → more power for near. Elasticity falls with age → presbyopia. Removing the lens (aphakia) loses over a third of the eye's power (cornea gives the rest).
points: Examine through a dilated pupil: slitlamp, or direct ophthalmoscope at +10 for red reflex.
chunks.hook: Squeeze the muscle, slacken the strings, fatten the lens.

cards.q: What happens to the zonules when the ciliary muscle contracts?
cards.a: Zonular tension relaxes, allowing the lens to become more spherical (accommodation).

chunks.title: Age-related cataract types
chunks.tldr: ~50% at 65–74, ~70% over 75. Risk: age, UV, smoking, diabetes, steroids, trauma. Nuclear sclerosis: yellow-brown nucleus, myopic shift ('second sight'), poor colour discrimination, monocular diplopia. Cortical: radial spokes/clefts from the equator (cuneiform, coronary); glare depends on position. Posterior subcapsular: plaque in visual axis → early glare and worse vision in bright light/reading; also from steroids, inflammation, radiation, trauma. Mature (all opaque), intumescent (swollen), hypermature (liquefied cortex, wrinkled capsule), Morgagnian (nucleus sinks in liquid cortex).
points: No drug has been shown to prevent or reverse cataract.
Surgery indication = symptoms and function, not a set acuity.
chunks.hook: Old patient suddenly reading without glasses = nuclear cataract myopic shift.

cards.q: Which cataract type gives early glare and worse vision in bright light?

cards.a: A hypermature cataract where the liquefied cortex lets the nucleus sink inferiorly in the capsular bag.

chunks.title: Childhood, traumatic & secondary cataract
chunks.tldr: Childhood: ⅓ hereditary, ⅓ metabolic/infectious/syndromic (rubella, galactosaemia, Lowe, Down), ⅓ unknown. Dense central unilateral cataract >2 mm must be removed within the first ~2 months or deprivation amblyopia is permanent; bilateral less urgent but operate both eyes close together. Leukocoria may be the sign; red reflex screening in nursery. Traumatic: blunt → posterior star/rosette, Vossius ring (iris pigment imprint); penetrating → rapid white lens (hammering metal on metal → IOFB). Complicated: uveitis, glaucoma, RP, RD → PSC. Systemic/drug: diabetes (snowflake), hypocalcaemia, myotonic dystrophy (Christmas tree), atopic, steroids, phenothiazines, amiodarone.
points: Zonular (lamellar) congenital cataract: one layer opaque, cortex clear.
chunks.hook: Baby with a dense one-sided cataract — the clock is ticking (6–8 weeks).

cards.a: Posterior subcapsular star/rosette-shaped cataract (± Vossius ring on the anterior capsule).

cards.q: Polychromatic 'Christmas tree' cataract suggests which disease?

chunks.title: Cataract surgery & IOLs
chunks.tldr: Extracapsular: keep the posterior capsule. Phaco: 2.5–3 mm incision, capsulorhexis, ultrasound breaks nucleus, aspirate cortex, foldable acrylic/silicone IOL in the bag (best position). MSICS: manual sutureless small incision, nucleus delivered whole — good for dense cataracts and low-resource settings. Femtosecond laser assistance: unproven routine benefit. Capsule tear → dropped nucleus (vitreoretinal surgery); IOL then sulcus or AC/sutured. Post-op: antibiotic + steroid drops 4–6 wk, shield at night.
points: Capsule tear risks: trauma, dense lens, zonular weakness (PXF), small pupil.
Multifocal IOLs give near + distance at the cost of halos/contrast.
chunks.hook: Bag is best — IOL in the capsular bag has the fewest complications.

cards.a: Manual small-incision cataract surgery: sutureless tunnel, nucleus removed intact, cortex aspirated manually — no phaco machine.

chunks.title: Complications of cataract surgery & PCO
chunks.tldr: Permanent vision-threatening complications only 2–5%. Worst: suprachoroidal haemorrhage (<0.5%) and endophthalmitis (~0.1%) → vitreous tap + intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftazidime), vitrectomy if severe. Others: RD, CME (Irvine-Gass), glaucoma, corneal oedema (pseudophakic bullous keratopathy), ptosis. Posterior capsule opacification ~10%: Elschnig pearls/fibrosis → Nd:YAG capsulotomy; risks IOP spike (check at ~3 h), IOL pitting, CME, RD.
points: Childhood surgery: primary posterior capsulotomy + anterior vitrectomy because PCO is near-universal; correct with CL or IOL (power hard to predict); glaucoma common long-term.
chunks.hook: Painful red eye days after phaco = endophthalmitis until proven otherwise — tap and inject.

cards.q: Most important first management of suspected post-cataract endophthalmitis?
cards.a: Vitreous tap for microscopy/culture and intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftazidime).

chunks.title: Dislocated lens
chunks.tldr: Hereditary (bilateral): Marfan (up & out, zonules stretched), homocystinuria (down & in, zonules disintegrate), Weill-Marchesani (small spherical lens, short stature), isolated familial. Traumatic: contusion. Signs: iridodonesis, phacodonesis, lens edge visible in pupil, deep/uneven AC; monocular diplopia, astigmatism. Complications: uveitis, glaucoma (pupil block, lens in AC). Leave alone if quiet and clear; else pars plana lensectomy/phaco with capsular tension ring or hooks.
chunks.hook: Marfan looks up at the stars; homocystinuria looks down at the floor.

cards.q: Direction of lens dislocation in Marfan vs homocystinuria?
cards.a: Marfan: superotemporal (up & out). Homocystinuria: inferonasal (down & in).
